connector: Hello, it’s Diana. Anne’s been invited to tea at the manse, all by herself, and she says it’s the most important thing that has ever happened to anybody. And next week I’m giving a party. Small and select, Anne calls it, just the girls in our class. Mother says we may play in the garden after tea. Everybody’s coming. Even Josie Pye.

guide2.label: Diana · before you open the book

rwm.label: Diana · about Read like a Writer

transcripts.welcome: Hello, it’s Diana. The question’s about pride, and how it makes people do dangerous things. I’ve known Anne a whole year now, and I’ll tell you, she has an awful lot of it. Today there’s a tea, and then there’s a party, and the party is at my house. Before all that there’s word work, and some sentences with more than one doing word in them. Find every one.
transcripts.wgrd: The box says every place lets you do some things and stops you doing others. That’s ever so true. At the manse Anne has to sit up straight and mind her manners. In our garden nobody’s minding anything. So as you read, keep asking what each place lets Anne do, and what it won’t. I know which place I’d rather be. I’m not sure Anne does.
transcripts.dol: The top sentence is Anne’s, word for word, and it’s awfully grand. Look at everything it does. The marks around her words, my name tucked in between commas, the period inside at the very end. The bottom one is two thoughts squashed together, one already done and one not yet. Give them each a sentence of their own. A stop, then a capital. And Anne’s name wants its capital too.
transcripts.guide1: Four bits of word work. Two you’ve seen before, so you’ll be quick. One asks you to tap every doing word that isn’t happening right now, and there’s more than one, so don’t stop at the first. The other asks for words that kept their y when you’d think it would change. Those are the sneaky ones. Ruby Gillis would tap everything in sight. Don’t be Ruby.
transcripts.morphology: Matching today. Two little word parts, and two word roots that go with them. One part means against. One means away, or down. The roots are the rest of words you already know. Say the whole word out loud, then take it apart. If you get stuck, think of coming down the stairs, or going away from home. Those two will tell you a great deal.
transcripts.vocabulary: These are the same four words as yesterday. Now you match them without the cards, and that’s the real test. Don’t just pick what sounds nice. Say each word in a sentence about someone you know. If it fits the person, you’ve likely got it. I said kindred about Anne and it fitted perfectly. Then I said it about Josie Pye. It did not.
transcripts.grammar: One long sentence, and lots of doing words in it. Some are already done and some haven’t happened yet. Tap every one that isn’t happening right now. There’s more than one, so keep going after the first. Read it slowly, a word at a time, and ask of each one, is this now? If it isn’t, tap it. Anne reads too fast. I read slowly, and I get things right.
transcripts.spelling: These words all ended in y once. Most changed it to an i when something got added. You don’t want those. You want the ones that kept their y when you might have expected it to change. So for each word, look at the letter in front of where the y was, and look at what got added. The y had a reason to stay. Find the ones with a reason.
transcripts.guide2: There’s a box here about being brave and being dared. I’ll tell you about daring, because everybody in Avonlea is doing it this summer. Somebody says you can’t, and then you simply have to. The boys started it, and now it’s us. It’s mostly silly things, climbing trees and hopping round gardens. Watch whether Anne picks the dare, or the dare picks Anne. I’m only saying watch.
transcripts.read: One stop, after the tea. Anne gets a letter with Miss on the front, and she can’t stop talking about it. Think about why one little word could matter so much to her. Then read on into my party. Watch the garden, and watch who dares whom, and in what order. The order matters more than you’d think. That’s all I’m going to say. Truly.
transcripts.rwm: That sentence is Anne coming up the lane with her letter, and it’s exactly how she moves when she’s happy. Like a sprite the wind is blowing about. The book doesn’t say she went fast. It says dancing, and then it gives you the sunshine and the shadows. When you write yours, choose the moving word first. Then the comparison. Then two things the place looks like.
transcripts.guide3: Oh, Anne. I begged her not to. I told her it wasn’t fair to dare anybody to do anything so dangerous. She had an answer ready, of course. She always does. When she fell I truly thought she was killed. She wasn’t. Now you write about it. Use what people said, the actual words, not what you think they meant. And don’t forget the tea. That was the nice part.
transcripts.chapter: The first question is about the tea, and it wants two details, not one. Look at what Mrs. Allan invites Anne to do. The second is about the roof. Look at who dared whom first, and then at what Anne says up there. The third is about Marilla. I didn’t see her face. I was looking at Anne. Find the line that tells you what hit Marilla. It’s a strong one.
transcripts.wordconn: Your grammar answer is saved. Read it again now. Anne said she would walk that ridgepole, and she did, a few steps anyway. Think about the word you picked. Was it something that already happened, or something somebody said would happen? Anne lives in both at once, mostly in the would. That’s why you have to keep an eye on her. I always do.
transcripts.workshop: This part is like the roof. Your kid wants something and is afraid of something, both at once, and everybody’s watching. Write it so the reader feels both. Then stop, right before your kid decides. Don’t tell what happens next. I couldn’t breathe, standing in our garden, not knowing. That’s what keeps a reader reading. Leave them standing in the garden too.

a.raw: anne climbed the ladder she will walk the ridgepole no matter what
a.fixed: Anne climbed the ladder. She will walk the ridgepole no matter what.
a.why: A capital on Anne, a period after the first thought (climbed is past), a capital S to start the next sentence (will walk is future), and a period at the end.

b.raw: anne opened the letter she will keep it forever
b.why: The same pattern: a capital on Anne, a period after the past-tense thought (opened), a capital S to start the future-tense one (will keep), and a period at the end.

scholar.journal-q1: … and say which detail would mean the most to Anne, and why.
scholar.journal-q2: … then say whether Anne could have walked away, and what it would have cost her.
scholar.journal-q3: … and say why it took a fright for Marilla to see it.

match.kindred: Kindred is Anne’s word for a person who feels about things the way she does. Look for the meaning about being alike inside.
match.precarious: Think of a ladder that wobbles under you. Look for the meaning about not being safe or steady.
match.vivacious: Vivacious has the root that means life in it. Look for the meaning about being full of life.
match.exquisite: Exquisite is a word for something so fine it’s almost fragile. Look for the meaning about delicate beauty.

notes.wgrd: Every place opens some doors and closes others. Ask what a place lets a character do, and what it stops them from doing.
vocab: Alike in spirit; sharing the same feelings, ideas, or imagination.
Unsafe; dangerously unsteady; not securely held in place.
Lively; full of energy and good spirits.
Beautiful in a delicate, refined way; very fine.
notes.wordParts: anti- means “against” or “opposite to” (antifreeze, antibody, antiseptic). de- means “away from” or “down” (depart, descend, decrease).
notes.grammar: Past tense tells what already happened: baked, arrived. Many past verbs end in -ed, but some don’t. Future tense tells what hasn’t happened yet: will + the plain verb, as in will bake.
notes.spelling: Change y to i before a suffix when a consonant comes before the y (happy → happier, story → stories). Keep the y when a vowel comes before it (play → played) and always before -ing (carry → carrying).
